title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in Dublin—meet in the middle!
description: We visualize routing on real street-map graphs from Dublin’s Smithfield toward a destination while Bidirectional Dijkstra expands from both ends. Watch how frontiers meet sooner than one-way search, reducing work while still guaranteeing optimal paths.
ig_caption:
🗺️🚦 Dublin (Smithfield) street graph search with **Bidirectional Dijkstra**!

Imagine each intersection as a node and each road segment as an edge with a nonnegative travel cost (time/distance). Instead of expanding only from the start like classic Dijkstra, we run two synchronized priority-queue searches:

➡️ **Forward Dijkstra** from the origin
⬅️ **Backward Dijkstra** from the destination (using the same nonnegative weights in reverse)

When the two expanding frontiers begin to overlap, we can derive the shortest path using the best combined distance found so far—often exploring dramatically fewer nodes than a single-source run. This is the “meet in the middle” idea from bidirectional search, while retaining Dijkstra’s optimality guarantees for weighted graphs. 📌

🚗💡 Ever wonder how route-finding stays fast *and* optimal? In this video we use **Bidirectional Dijkstra** to search a real street-map graph in Dublin (Smithfield) by expanding from both the start and the goal at the same time. 

Graph search tip: because edges (roads) have **nonnegative weights**, two Dijkstra frontiers can meet and we can combine their best distances to recover the shortest path efficiently. You’ll see how bidirectional search reduces explored nodes while preserving the shortest-path guarantee on weighted graphs with nonnegative edge costs.
